6530:
Foulmouthed describes a person who regularly and habitually uses offensive, vulgar, or crude language — such as swear words, obscene expressions, and deeply inappropriate words — especially in situations where such language is considered shocking or disrespectful.

Think of it this way: foul means dirty, disgusting, or offensive. Mouthed points to what comes out of a person's mouth — their speech. Put them together, and a foulmouthed person is essentially someone with a "dirty mouth" — someone whose words are consistently crude, obscene, or deeply offensive to others.

Not every person who swears occasionally is foulmouthed. The word carries a specific weight. Here's what it really captures:

  • Frequency matters. A foulmouthed person doesn't just slip up with a bad word once in a while. They use offensive language constantly and freely, as a regular feature of how they speak.
  • It is a character trait. When you call someone foulmouthed, you are describing something about their personality or habit — not just one bad moment. It is the kind of thing you'd say about someone in general, not about a single outburst.
  • The language is genuinely offensive. It goes beyond mild swearing. A foulmouthed person uses words that are vulgar (sexually crude), profane (disrespectful of things held sacred), or simply deeply rude — words that make others uncomfortable, shocked, or offended.
  • There is little self-awareness or filter. A foulmouthed person often does not adjust their language based on who is listening — whether it is a child, an elder, a stranger, or someone in a formal setting. They say whatever crude thing comes to mind.
The Tone and Attitude of the Word

"Foulmouthed" is a judgmental word. When you call someone foulmouthed, you are expressing disapproval. It is not a neutral description — it signals that the speaker finds the person's language unpleasant, offensive, or socially unacceptable.

It is similar in feeling to calling someone "rude" or "crude" — you are passing a small verdict on their behavior.
How It Is Used in Sentences

Here are examples that show the word in action:

  • "He was a brilliant comedian but completely foulmouthed — every other word was a curse."
  • "The children's parents complained about the foulmouthed neighbor who yelled in the street."
  • "She warned me her boss was foulmouthed, so I wasn't too shocked during the meeting."
  • "Despite his foulmouthed reputation, he somehow managed to charm everyone at the party."
  • "The film was criticized for its foulmouthed dialogue, which many felt was unnecessary."

Notice in the last example that "foulmouthed" is used to describe dialogue (speech in a film), not a person. This is perfectly natural — the word can describe language, remarks, or speech itself, not just the speaker.

Like most descriptive words, foulmouthed can exist on a spectrum:

  • Someone can be mildly foulmouthed — they swear more than most people but it isn't extreme.
  • Someone can be notoriously or aggressively foulmouthed — their language is so vulgar and constant that it is one of the first things anyone notices about them.

You can intensify it with adverbs:

  • "He was outrageously foulmouthed."
  • "She was surprisingly foulmouthed for someone in her position."

These words overlap with "foulmouthed" but each has a slightly different flavor:

  • Crude — focuses on a general lack of refinement or social grace in speech (and behavior).
  • Vulgar — specifically highlights sexually coarse or obscene language.
  • Profane — emphasizes the use of words that are considered blasphemous or irreverent toward sacred things.
  • Obscene — the strongest of these words; refers to language that is deeply offensive, often in a sexual or disturbing way.
  • Foul-tongued — a rarer synonym that means essentially the same thing as foulmouthed.

If someone is NOT foulmouthed, you might describe them as:

  • Clean-spoken or clean-mouthed — they avoid offensive language.
  • Well-spoken — they speak in a polished, respectful way.
  • Refined or civil — their language is appropriate and controlled.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

Foulmouthed = a person (or their speech) characterized by the frequent, habitual use of offensive, crude, or vulgar language. It is a disapproving word, used to judge someone's speech habits negatively. It describes a pattern, not a single instance.

If you remember just one image: picture someone who has no "filter" between their mind and their mouth — and what comes out is consistently crude, rude, and offensive. That is a foulmouthed person.
6531: The word "found" works as a verb in two completely separate ways. They share the same spelling but are unrelated in meaning.

This is the most common use. "Found" is what "find" becomes when you talk about the past.

"Find" means to come across something, to discover something, or to come to know something. When this action happened in the past, you use "found."

As a simple past (an action completed in the past):

  • "I found my keys under the sofa."
  • "She found a job last month."
  • "He found peace after years of struggle."
  • "They found that the door was unlocked."

As a past participle (used with helping verbs like have/has/had, or in passive sentences):

  • "I have found the answer." — present perfect (the action is done and matters now)
  • "She has found a great doctor."
  • "The treasure was found by a young boy." — passive (someone found it, and the focus is on the treasure, not the finder)
  • "I had found the mistake before anyone else noticed." — past perfect (found it before some other past event)

The rule is simple: whenever "find" is used in the past — with or without a helping verb — it becomes "found."
Meaning 2: To found — to establish or create something formally

This is a completely different verb, entirely unrelated to "find." "To found" means to establish, set up, or bring into existence an institution, organization, country, city, company, or movement. It implies creating something from scratch, with a purpose, that is meant to last.

Examples:

  • "He founded the company in 1995." (He created and established it.)
  • "The United States was founded in 1776." (It was formally established then.)
  • "She founded a school for children with disabilities." (She built it from nothing, with vision and purpose.)
  • "The two brothers founded the organization together."

Notice that in the past tense, this verb uses "founded," not "found." In the present tense, it's "found" (or "founds" for he/she/it), but you'll rarely encounter it that way because we almost always talk about founding in the past:

  • "Every year, the group founds a new community center." ✅ (grammatically fine, but rare)

What makes "found" different from just "start" or "create"?

"Found" carries a sense of formality, permanence, and intention. You don't say "She founded a sandwich for lunch." You say "She made a sandwich." But you say "She founded a company" because a company is a formal institution intended to exist over time. "Founded" is specifically used when someone is the original creator — the one who brought something into existence for the very first time, usually with a clear vision or mission.

Common things that are "founded":

  • a company / organization / institution
  • a city / nation / state
  • a movement / religion / dynasty
  • a school / university / hospital

Words born from this verb:

  • founder (noun) — a person who founds something; "the founder of Apple"
  • co-founder (noun) — someone who founds something together with others
  • founding (adjective) — relating to the act of establishing; "the founding fathers"
  • foundation (noun) — the act of founding, or a formally created charitable organization; "the foundation of the city"; "a charitable foundation"
Meaning 3 (rare and technical): To melt and cast metal

In industrial or historical contexts, "to found" can also mean to melt metal and pour it into a mold to give it a shape. This is where the word foundry (a factory where metal objects are cast) comes from. You're very unlikely to meet this meaning in everyday reading or conversation, but knowing it exists means you won't be confused if you do come across it.
The one confusion you must avoid

Because "found" (past of "find") and "founded" (past of "to found/establish") sound and look similar, people sometimes mix them up in passive sentences. Here's the key difference:

  • "The body was found in the river." → discovered (passive of "find") ✅
  • "The body was founded in the river." → ❌ this makes no sense
  • "The company was founded in 1990." → established (passive of "to found") ✅
  • "The company was found in 1990." → ❌ this is wrong; it would mean someone discovered the company

The test is simple: if you can replace the word with "discovered," use "found." If you can replace it with "established" or "created," use "founded."

What it meansExample
Past of "find"To have discovered or come across something"I found my bag."
To found (present)To establish something new and lasting(rare) "They found a new club."
Founded (past of "to found")Established or created formally"He founded the company."

That is everything there is to know about "found" as a verb — both its common everyday use as the past of "find," and its distinct meaning of formally establishing something that endures.
6532:
Foundation means the base or support that everything else is built upon or depends on. It is the thing that comes first, sits underneath, and holds everything else up. If the foundation is weak or missing, whatever rests on it will collapse or fail.

This single idea — a supporting base — runs through every meaning of this word, whether you are talking about a building, an idea, an organization, or your face.
Meaning 1: The Physical Base of a Building

This is the most literal and original meaning. The foundation of a building is the solid structure underneath it — usually made of concrete, stone, or brick — that is dug into the ground and supports the entire weight of the building above it.

The workers spent three weeks pouring concrete to lay the foundation before the walls could go up.

You never see a building's foundation once construction is complete, because it is buried underground. But without it, the building would sink, crack, or fall over. It is invisible but absolutely essential.

This physical meaning is the anchor for all the other meanings of the word.
Meaning 2: The Basis of an Idea, Belief, or System

When used abstractly, foundation refers to the core principle, fact, or belief that something is built on — the starting point from which everything else follows. Just like a building rests on its physical foundation, ideas, arguments, societies, and relationships rest on their intellectual or moral foundations.

Trust is the foundation of any healthy relationship.
The foundation of science is the belief that the world operates according to consistent, discoverable rules.
Her entire argument had no foundation — she couldn't back up a single claim.

When someone says an argument is "without foundation" or "has no foundation," they mean it has no solid base of evidence or logic — it is just floating in thin air, unsupported.

Some common phrases you will encounter:

  • "lay the foundation for something" — to do the early, preparatory work that makes something bigger possible later.

    Her years of reading laid the foundation for her brilliant writing career.

  • "shake/undermine the foundations of something" — to challenge or damage the core principles that something depends on.

    The scandal shook the foundations of public trust in the government.

  • "on a solid/firm/shaky foundation" — to describe how well-supported or stable something is.

    Their friendship was built on a shaky foundation of convenience rather than genuine connection.
Meaning 3: The Act of Establishing Something

Foundation can also refer to the act of creating or establishing an institution, organization, city, or system — the moment it was "founded" (started).

The foundation of the United States as a nation is dated to 1776.
The foundation of the university took place over two hundred years ago.

In this sense, the word describes the beginning moment — the act of bringing something into existence.
Meaning 4: A Charitable or Non-Profit Organization

A foundation can be a type of organization, usually non-profit, that is set up to support a cause — often through giving money to research, education, the arts, healthcare, or the poor.

The Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation funds global health and education programs.
She donated all her prize money to a foundation that supports cancer research.

These organizations are called "foundations" because they aim to provide a base of support for important work in society. They are typically created with a large sum of money (called an endowment) that is used to fund their activities over time.
Meaning 5: Foundation as a Cosmetic Product

In the world of makeup and beauty, foundation (also called "foundation makeup") is a skin-colored cosmetic product applied to the face to even out the skin tone, cover blemishes, and create a smooth, uniform appearance. It comes in liquid, cream, powder, or stick form.

She applied foundation before adding any other makeup.
Finding the right shade of foundation to match your skin tone can be tricky.

It is called "foundation" because it is the first layer applied to the skin — the base upon which all other makeup (blush, eyeshadow, lipstick) is then built. It is, literally, the foundation of your makeup.

No matter which meaning you encounter, the word foundation always carries the same essential idea: something that comes first, goes underneath, and makes everything else possible.

SituationWhat the "foundation" is

When talking about a building, the foundation is the concrete base underground. When talking about a relationship or a country, the foundation is the core values and trust that hold it together. When talking about a charity, the foundation is the organized structure and funding that supports a cause. When talking about makeup, the foundation is the first layer of cosmetic applied to the skin.

In all cases, the word signals: this is the bottom, the beginning, the support — and without it, what comes above cannot stand.
Words That Are Close in Meaning

It helps to know how foundation sits alongside similar words:

  • Base — very similar in meaning, and often interchangeable, but "base" tends to be more physical and concrete. "Foundation" carries a slightly weightier, more formal, or more conceptual feel.

    "The base of the statue" vs. "the foundation of democracy" — both work, but foundation feels more elevated in abstract contexts.

  • Basis — almost identical in abstract uses, but "basis" is usually reserved for ideas, reasons, and arguments. You would say "on the basis of the evidence" not "on the foundation of the evidence" — though both are grammatically possible.
  • Groundwork — refers specifically to the early preparatory work done before something bigger is built. Laying the groundwork is similar to laying the foundation, but "groundwork" emphasizes the process and effort, while "foundation" emphasizes the resulting base.
  • Bedrock — a more emphatic, often poetic version. When something is described as the bedrock of a belief or society, it means it is the deepest and most unshakeable foundation of all.

Foundation (noun) means the supportive base — physical, intellectual, or organizational — upon which something else is built, stands, or depends. It can be:

  1. The physical concrete/stone base of a building
  2. The core idea, value, or fact that supports a system, argument, or relationship
  3. The act of establishing or starting an institution
  4. A non-profit organization created to support a cause
  5. The first layer of makeup applied to the face

Whatever the context, the word tells you: this is where it begins, and this is what holds the rest up.
6533:
Imagine building a house. Before the walls, the roof, the windows, or the rooms — workers first lay down a strong concrete base deep in the ground. This is called the foundation. Everything above it rests on it, depends on it, and would collapse without it.

"Foundational" is the adjective form of "foundation." It describes anything — an idea, a skill, a principle, a decision, a document — that plays the same role as that concrete base. It is the thing that comes first, holds everything else up, and makes everything else possible.

So when you call something foundational, you are saying two things at once:

  1. This thing is essential — you cannot remove it without everything else falling apart.
  2. This thing is a base — other things are built on top of it and depend on it.
Why "foundational" is stronger than just saying "important"

Lots of things are important. A good teacher is important. Sleep is important. But "important" just means something matters a lot.

"Foundational" means something more specific. It means the thing is a structural base — other things rest on it and wouldn't exist or work without it. Think of it this way:

  • A roof is important in a house. But it is not foundational — it sits on top. If you remove the roof, the walls still stand.
  • The foundation, however, is what the entire structure sits on. Remove it, and everything above collapses.

This is the key instinct to carry with you: something foundational is not just highly valued — it is load-bearing. Other things depend on it.
How It Is Used Across Different Areas of Life

The beauty of "foundational" is that it travels across almost every domain. Here are the major ones:

1. Learning and Education

Before you can write an essay, you need to know grammar. Before you learn grammar, you need to know the alphabet and basic words. These earliest skills — the ones everything later depends on — are called foundational skills.

"Reading and writing are foundational skills for all other academic learning."

This means: you cannot meaningfully learn history, science, or anything else if you cannot read. Reading supports everything.

2. Knowledge and Science

In any field, there are a small number of ideas so important that all other knowledge in that field is built on them. These are called foundational concepts, foundational theories, or foundational principles.

"Newton's laws of motion are foundational to classical physics."

This means every other principle in classical physics either comes from Newton's laws or relies on them to make sense.

3. Values and Beliefs

A person's foundational beliefs are their deepest, most basic convictions — the ones that shape every other opinion and decision they make. If someone's foundational belief is that all people deserve equal dignity, that one belief will influence how they treat others, how they vote, what they stand up for, and so on.

"Her foundational belief in fairness shaped every decision she made as a leader."

4. Law and Society

Some documents or agreements are so central to a system that all other rules must align with them.

"The Constitution is foundational to the American legal system."

This means every other law must be consistent with the Constitution. It is the base — not just the oldest document, but the one everything else must answer to.

5. Decisions and Actions

Early decisions in a project, company, or relationship can be foundational because they set the direction that everything afterward follows.

"The foundational decision to put customers first shaped the entire company culture for decades."

Here, one early choice became the base on which the whole culture was built.
The Two Qualities Every Foundational Thing Has

No matter the context, something truly foundational always has both of these qualities:

Quality 1 — It comes first (logically or structurally).
It is at the bottom, at the beginning, at the root. Other things build on top of it. You cannot skip it and come back to it later — you need it from the start.

Quality 2 — Other things depend on it.
If you take it away, the things above it either fall apart, stop making sense, or cannot function properly. The dependency runs in one direction: the higher things need the foundational thing, not the other way around.

If something is important but does not have both these qualities, you probably should not call it "foundational."
Foundational vs. Words That Look Similar

These words are close cousins of "foundational," but each has a slightly different flavor:

Basic — means simple, entry-level. Something can be basic without being foundational (e.g., a basic recipe is simple, but other recipes don't depend on it). And something foundational is not always simple — it can be complex. The key difference is that "foundational" always implies that other things rest on it.

Fundamental — this is the closest word to "foundational" in everyday use, and the two are often interchangeable. However, "fundamental" tends to emphasize that something is deeply essential by its very nature, while "foundational" slightly more strongly evokes the image of a base layer that others are built upon. In practice, most native speakers treat them as equivalent.

Essential — means absolutely necessary. But "essential" doesn't carry the structural image of a base. Oxygen is essential to human life, but we don't usually call it foundational because nothing is "built on top of" oxygen. "Foundational" adds the layered structure idea.

Core — refers to the center or heart of something. A core belief is at the center of your thinking. A foundational belief is the base your other beliefs stand on. Both can describe the same thing, but from different angles: "core" = central; "foundational" = load-bearing base.

Primary — means first in order or rank. Being primary doesn't automatically mean other things depend on it. "Foundational" always involves that dependency.
A Few More Natural Examples to Solidify the Word

• "Trust is foundational to any healthy relationship." → Without trust, the relationship has no stable base to stand on; everything else in it becomes shaky.
  • "These early mathematics lessons are foundational — students will use them every day for the rest of their education."
  • "The company's foundational values were honesty, innovation, and respect." → These values were set at the very beginning and every policy, hiring decision, and product choice was built on top of them.
  • "Understanding supply and demand is foundational to studying economics." → You cannot understand more advanced economic ideas until you have this one.
One-Line Test to Know If Something Is "Foundational"

Ask yourself: "If I remove this, do the things that depend on it fall apart or stop making sense?"

If yes — it is foundational.
If no — it may be important, but probably not foundational.

Foundational means: serving as the essential base or starting point upon which other things are built and depend. It is the adjective for anything that plays the role of a foundation — the deep, structural layer that holds everything above it up. Without something foundational, what rests on it weakens, collapses, or loses its meaning. It is used across education, science, law, belief systems, relationships, and organizations to describe the most essential, load-bearing elements of any structure — physical or abstract.
6534:
A founder is a person who creates something — brings it into existence from nothing — and establishes it as a lasting entity. The "something" is typically an organization, institution, company, movement, city, or nation.

The single most important idea behind this word is this: a founder is present at the moment of creation. They are the one who makes the thing begin to exist. Without them, that particular thing would not have started when it did, in the way that it did.

People use the word founder across many contexts:

  • Companies and businesses — Mark Zuckerberg is the founder of Facebook (now Meta). Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak are the founders of Apple.
  • Organizations and institutions — A charity, a university, a hospital, a political party, or a club all have founders.
  • Cities and nations — Historically, the people who first established a city or country are called its founders. The men who created and established the United States (Washington, Jefferson, Hamilton, and others) are called the Founding Fathers.
  • Religions and movements — The Buddha is considered the founder of Buddhism. A person who starts a social movement or a new school of thought can also be called its founder.

So the word is not limited to business — it applies anywhere something new and organized is brought into being.
The Essence: What Makes Someone a Founder?

Three things define a founder:

  1. Initiative — They decided to start the thing. They didn't join something already running; they are the reason it started at all.
  2. Creation from scratch — They brought the entity into existence when it did not exist before.
  3. Establishment — They didn't just have an idea; they actually set it up, gave it shape, and made it a real, functioning thing.

A key insight: the title of "founder" is permanent and historical. Even if a founder later leaves the company, gets fired, sells their share, or passes away — they remain the founder forever. It describes a role at a specific moment in history, and that moment cannot be erased. For example, even though Steve Jobs left Apple for several years and then returned, he has always been and will always be a founder of Apple.

These distinctions will sharpen your understanding significantly:

Founder vs. Owner
You can buy ownership of a company or organization you had no part in creating. But you cannot buy the title of "founder." Ownership can be transferred; founding cannot. A person who buys a bakery is the owner, not the founder, unless they started it themselves.

Founder vs. CEO / President / Director
These are roles — positions of leadership that can be held by anyone, including people who joined the organization years after it was created. A founder may also be the CEO, but the two are separate things. Many companies have a founder who is no longer the CEO. Equally, many CEOs are not founders.

Founder vs. Inventor
An inventor creates a product, a technology, or an idea. A founder creates an organization. These can overlap — someone might invent a product and then found a company to sell it — but they are different acts. Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone. He also co-founded a company around it (AT&T's predecessor). Both titles are valid, but they describe different things he did.

Founder vs. Pioneer
A pioneer is someone who is among the first to do something in a broad field — like a pioneer of aviation or a pioneer of modern medicine. It doesn't require creating a specific organization. A founder, on the other hand, is specifically tied to the creation of a particular entity.

When two or more people start something together, each of them is called a co-founder (short for co-founder, meaning joint founder). Collectively, they can all be referred to as "the founders."

For example, Google was co-founded by Larry Page and Sergey Brin — both of them created it together, so both hold the title of co-founder.

In casual and common usage, people often drop the "co-" and just say "founder" for all of them. Both usages are acceptable.

• "Founding member" — One of the original members when a group, club, or organization was first formed. Slightly different from founder — you can be a founding member without having been the one who initiated everything, as long as you were there at the very start.
  • "Founding father" — Used for the creators of nations, institutions, or important movements. In the US context, it specifically refers to the leaders who established the country.
  • "Founder and CEO" — A common title in business meaning the person both started the company and currently leads it.
  • "Founders' equity" / "Founders' shares" — In business and startups, these refer to the ownership stake given to the people who started the company, usually a significantly large portion because they took the risk of building from nothing.
The Implicit Weight of the Word

The word founder carries a sense of vision, risk, and responsibility. Founders typically:

  • Take on personal risk (financial, reputational, time) to start something with no guarantee of success.
  • Shape the original values, culture, and direction of what they create.
  • Are often deeply tied to the identity of the thing they founded — people associate the organization with them.

This is why the word is used with a degree of respect. Being called a founder signals that you built something from nothing.

A founder is the person (or one of the people) who originally created and established an organization, institution, company, movement, or similar entity — making them permanently and historically the one responsible for bringing it into existence.
6535: To founder means to sink, collapse, or fail completely — and almost always permanently. It describes something that doesn't just hit a rough patch, but actually goes under and is finished.
The Different Contexts It's Used In

1. Ships — the most literal meaning

When a ship founders, it takes on water and sinks to the bottom of the sea. This is the oldest, most physical use of the word.

"The cargo ship foundered in the storm, and the crew had to be rescued."

2. Plans, projects, businesses, relationships — the most common modern use

This is how you'll encounter it most often. When a plan, negotiation, or business founders, it collapses completely — because it ran into a serious obstacle it simply couldn't get past.

"The peace talks foundered when neither side would compromise."
"Their startup foundered after it ran out of funding."
"The friendship foundered over a bitter argument that was never resolved."

Notice that the obstacle can be dramatic (a war, a bankruptcy) or quiet (a slow erosion of trust). What matters is the outcome: it's over, it's done.

3. Horses — a specialized use

A horse is said to founder when it develops a painful foot condition (called laminitis) that makes it go lame. You'll mainly see this in contexts involving farming, equestrian sports, or veterinary care.

"The horse foundered after eating too much rich grass."

4. Buildings and ground — rare but valid

A structure can founder when the ground beneath it shifts and it sinks or collapses.

"The old building foundered as the waterlogged soil beneath it gave way."
The Most Important Thing to Understand

Founder always implies finality. Whatever founders is not merely struggling — it is going down completely. A ship that founders is at the bottom of the sea. A business that founders has not just lost money — it has collapsed. A negotiation that founders is not paused — it is dead.

This is what gives the word its weight. When a writer chooses "foundered," they're telling you: this thing is gone.
The One Mistake Everyone Makes: Founder vs. Flounder

These two words are constantly confused — even by native speakers. Getting this right is essential.

Flounder means to struggle and thrash about without making progress. The thing or person is still going — just badly and awkwardly.

Founder means to collapse entirely. It's over.

Here's a clear way to see the difference:

A swimmer who is floundering is struggling in the water — panicking, swallowing water, failing to swim properly — but they are still there, still fighting. A ship that is foundering is sinking to the bottom. It will soon be gone.

In everyday life: a company that is floundering is having serious trouble but its doors are still open. A company that has foundered has shut down completely.

The quick test: Is it still going, just badly? → flounder. Has it completely collapsed and is there no coming back? → founder.

The verb founder is a word that carries real weight. Whether it's a ship filling with water, a political negotiation falling apart over an irreconcilable difference, or a years-long relationship finally breaking down — "founder" always delivers the same verdict: this did not merely struggle. It went under. And it isn't coming back.
6536: A foundry is a factory or workshop where metal is melted into liquid form and then poured into molds to create solid metal objects of specific shapes. Think of it like a large-scale kitchen — but instead of baking cookie dough into shaped cookies, workers pour glowing, liquid metal into shaped containers and wait for it to cool and harden. The finished object produced this way is called a casting, and the process is called casting or founding.

The work follows a clear sequence:

1. Melting — Workers load solid metal (iron, steel, aluminum, bronze, etc.) into a powerful industrial furnace. The furnace heats the metal to extreme temperatures — often above 1,500°C — until it becomes a flowing liquid.

2. Molding — Workers prepare a mold: a shaped hollow cavity that will define the final form of the object. Molds are often made from tightly packed sand mixed with a binding agent, or sometimes from metal itself.

3. Pouring — The molten metal is carefully ladled or poured into the mold, filling the cavity completely.

4. Cooling — The metal is left to cool and solidify. Depending on the size and type of metal, this can take anywhere from a few minutes to several hours.

5. Removal and finishing — Once solid, the casting is taken out of the mold, cleaned up, and any rough leftover edges (called flash) are trimmed away. The finished piece is then ready to use or to be machined further into something more precise.

Foundries produce objects that need to be strong, heavy, or have complex shapes that would be difficult or expensive to cut out of a solid block of metal. Examples:

  • Engine blocks and cylinder heads for cars, trucks, and heavy machinery
  • Pipes, valves, and fittings for plumbing and industrial systems
  • Manhole covers on streets and roads
  • Bells — large church bells have traditionally been cast in specialist bell foundries
  • Statues and sculptures — art foundries cast bronze artworks, monuments, and figurines
  • Cast iron cookware — pans and pots
  • Machine parts of every kind imaginable

Different metals require different equipment, so foundries are often categorized by the metal they work with:

  • Iron foundries — the most historically significant kind, working with cast iron, a strong and affordable material used in construction and machinery for centuries
  • Steel foundries — work with steel, which is tougher and more versatile
  • Aluminum foundries — work with lightweight aluminum, heavily used in the automotive and aerospace industries
  • Non-ferrous foundries — work with copper-based alloys like bronze and brass; many art foundries fall into this category

A foundry can be a small artisan workshop where a single craftsperson hand-pours metal into molds, or it can be a vast industrial complex employing thousands of people and producing millions of parts every year. The word covers the full spectrum.

Because the idea of creating something from raw material through a specialized shaping process is so central to the word, "foundry" has been adopted by other industries as well.

Type foundry — In printing and typography, a type foundry originally referred to a workshop where individual metal letters (called "type") were cast for use in printing presses. These tiny metal letters were what printers assembled to form words on a page. Today, the term has carried forward: a type foundry now means a company that designs and sells typefaces (fonts). The physical casting is long gone, but the spirit of "crafting letterforms" remains. Well-known type foundries include Monotype and Hoefler&Co, as well as hundreds of independent studios.

Semiconductor foundry / chip foundry — In the technology industry, a "foundry" refers to a factory that manufactures computer chips. Just as a metal foundry takes a design and produces a physical object, a chip foundry takes a circuit design from a technology company and manufactures the actual silicon chips. The company does not design the chip — it only manufactures it on behalf of others. The most famous example is TSMC (Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company), which manufactures chips designed by Apple, NVIDIA, AMD, and many others. This sense of the word is extremely common in technology news and business reporting today.

• "The iron foundry at the edge of town has been running for over a hundred years." → A traditional metal-casting factory.
  • "She sent her clay sculpture model to a bronze foundry to have it cast." → An art foundry.
  • "The bell was cast at a foundry in the Netherlands." → A specialist bell foundry.
  • "Apple's chips are manufactured at a foundry in Taiwan." → A semiconductor chip foundry.
  • "They licensed the typeface from a boutique type foundry in Berlin." → A font design company.
The One Idea That Ties It All Together

No matter which sense of the word you encounter, a foundry is always a place where something is created through a controlled process of shaping raw material into a finished product — whether that raw material is iron ore, liquid bronze, or a circuit design. The original and most common meaning is always the metal-casting factory, and every other use of the word is borrowing that same image of skilled workers transforming something formless into something precise and useful.
6537:
A fount is a source — specifically, a rich, generous, and seemingly endless source from which something flows. Think of it like a spring of water that never runs dry. Whatever flows from a fount flows naturally, abundantly, and from a deep origin.

The word carries a slightly formal, literary feel. You are more likely to read it in a book or a speech than hear it in everyday conversation.

"Fount" has three distinct meanings as a noun. Two are general, one is technical.

Meaning 1: A Spring or Source of Water (Literal)

In its most literal sense, a fount is a natural spring — a place where water flows up from the ground, or a fountain. This is its oldest use and the physical image that gives the word its power.

"They rested beside a fount of clear, cool water deep in the forest."

You will not encounter this literal use very often in modern writing. It tends to appear in poetry, old literature, or religious texts. But understanding this image — water gushing up naturally from a source — is the key to understanding everything else the word does.

Meaning 2: A Source of Something in Abundance (Figurative)

This is by far the most common and important meaning of "fount" today. Here, "fount" is used figuratively to describe a person, place, or thing that is a rich and seemingly endless source of something — usually something good or valuable, like knowledge, wisdom, inspiration, or creativity.

The critical idea is that a fount is not just any source. It suggests:

  • Depth — the source is deep, not shallow
  • Abundance — it gives generously, not sparingly
  • Originality — it is a primary or fundamental source, not second-hand

Think of it this way: if knowledge were water, a fount of knowledge would be the underground spring, not the cup someone poured it into.

"My grandmother was a fount of stories about our family's past."
"The professor is considered a fount of wisdom on this subject."
"Great universities should be founts of new ideas."

The phrase "fount of all knowledge" deserves special mention because it is extremely common. It is used in two ways:

  • Sincerely: to praise someone who seems to know an enormous amount about everything.
    "Ask Dr. Ellis — she's a fount of all knowledge when it comes to biology."
  • Sarcastically or humorously: to mock someone who acts like they know everything, or to poke fun at yourself.
    "Oh, don't ask me — I'm hardly the fount of all knowledge."

You can tell from context which one is meant.

Meaning 3: A Complete Set of Printing Type (Technical — British English)

In the world of printing and typography, particularly in British English, fount (also sometimes spelled font) refers to a complete set of metal type characters all belonging to the same style and size — for example, all the letters, numbers, and punctuation marks in a specific typeface at a specific size.

"The printer ordered a new fount of bold italic type for the press."

Important note: In everyday modern usage — especially in computing and design — the word "font" has almost completely replaced "fount" for this meaning. When you change the font on your computer, the word you're using is directly related to this old printing sense of "fount." If you encounter "fount" in this technical sense, it will almost always be in an older British text about physical printing.
The Tone and Register of the Word

"Fount" is not a word you use casually. It sits in formal, literary, or elevated language. It lends a sense of grandeur or depth to what you are describing.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "She is a source of good advice." — neutral, plain, everyday
  • "She is a fount of good advice." — elevated, warm, slightly poetic, implies her advice is deep and abundant

The meaning is similar, but "fount" makes the second sentence feel more significant and expressive.

It helps to draw clear lines between "fount" and words that look or feel similar:

  • Source — the plain, everyday, all-purpose word for where something comes from. "Fount" is a more literary and expressive version of "source."
  • Fountain — in everyday speech, a fountain is a decorative water structure in a park or a square. "Fount" is the more poetic, stripped-down form of the same idea.
  • Font (in churches) — a font is the basin inside a church that holds holy water used for baptism. This is a closely related word with a shared history, but "font" in this sense and "fount" are used in different contexts and are not interchangeable today.
  • Font (in computing/design) — the digital typeface you choose on your computer. This descends from the printing sense of "fount" but is now its own fully separate word in practice.

You will most often see "fount" followed by "of" and then a noun describing something valuable:

  • a fount of knowledge
  • a fount of wisdom
  • a fount of inspiration
  • a fount of information
  • a fount of creativity
  • a fount of goodness / kindness
  • a fount of all knowledge (the most famous phrase)

It almost always describes something positive, rich, and deep. You would not naturally say "a fount of problems" or "a fount of noise" — the word pulls toward abundance of something worthwhile.

LiteralA spring or source of water
Figurative (main use)A rich, deep, and abundant source of something valuable
Technical (British printing)A complete set of type in one style and size
ToneFormal, literary, elevated
Most common phrase"a fount of knowledge / wisdom"

Once you understand that the soul of this word is "a deep and overflowing source," every use of it — literal, figurative, or technical — will immediately make sense to you.
6538:
Imagine a mountain spring — a single point in the earth where water pushes up from deep underground and begins to flow. Everything downstream — the stream, the river, the waterfall — exists because of that one original point. That point is the fountainhead. It is the chief, original source from which everything else flows.

This is the heart of the word: the primary source from which something originates and spreads outward.

1. The Literal Meaning

In a purely physical sense, a fountainhead is the natural spring or source from which a river or stream begins. It is the very first point where the water emerges. This usage is rare in modern conversation but helps you feel the word's soul.

2. The Figurative Meaning (How It's Actually Used)

This is where the word truly lives. In everyday language, "fountainhead" is used to describe the original, primary source of an idea, movement, tradition, culture, or creative force — the thing from which everything else in a particular domain flows.

Think of it this way: just as a river can be traced back to its source spring, many great things in human life — philosophies, art movements, political revolutions, scientific schools of thought — can be traced back to a single, powerful origin point. That origin point is the fountainhead.
What Makes It Special (vs. Just Saying "Source")

The word "source" is broad and ordinary. A fountainhead is not just any source — it carries three very specific ideas packed inside it:

  • Primacy — it is the first and original source, not a secondary or later one.
  • Power — it is the chief source; the most important and influential one.
  • Flow — everything else comes from it and spreads outward, like water flowing from a spring.

So when someone calls something a fountainhead, they are saying: "This is the single, most fundamental origin point. Everything else in this area grew from here."
Examples That Show It in Action

• "Ancient Greece is the fountainhead of Western philosophy."

This means Western philosophy didn't just begin in Greece — Greece is the single original source from which all of Western philosophical thought has flowed ever since. Aristotle, Plato, Socrates — everything came from that one spring.

  • "Einstein was the fountainhead of modern theoretical physics."

His ideas were not merely influential — they were the original source from which an entirely new way of understanding physics emerged and spread to others.

  • "That small jazz club in New Orleans was the fountainhead of an entire musical revolution."

The club wasn't just important to jazz; it was the point of origin from which the whole movement began flowing outward into the world.

  • "The printing press was the fountainhead of the information age."

Before the press, information could not spread freely. The press was the original source — the spring — from which the flow of mass communication began.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

"Fountainhead" is a serious, powerful, somewhat elevated word. You will find it in literature, academic writing, journalism, and speeches — not in casual texting. When someone uses it, they are signaling that they are talking about something of great importance and deep origin.

It almost always carries a sense of admiration or gravity. Calling something a fountainhead is a way of paying it a high compliment — saying it is not just important, but foundationally important, the very spring from which something great emerged.

Ayn Rand's 1943 novel The Fountainhead takes its title directly from this concept. The novel's hero, an architect named Howard Roark, represents a human being who is his own fountainhead — his own original, independent source of ideas, values, and creative power. He draws nothing from others and owes his thinking to no tradition. Rand used the word to capture the idea of a person who is an original source unto themselves, not a follower of any stream that came before. This is perhaps the most famous use of the word in modern culture, and knowing it deepens your feel for the word's power.
A fountainhead is the single, original, most powerful source from which something great — an idea, a movement, a tradition, a force — first emerges and then flows outward into the world.
6539:
A fowl is a bird — but not just any bird in any situation. The word is almost always used for birds that are closely connected to humans, particularly birds that are kept, raised, or hunted for food (their meat or eggs) or sometimes for their feathers.

Think of a chicken. That is the perfect, classic example of a fowl. When you picture a farm with hens clucking around, those birds are fowl.
The range of meaning: from broad to narrow

The word "fowl" doesn't mean just one single thing. It stretches across a range of meanings depending on context. Here is how to understand that range:

1. The broadest meaning — any bird at all

In old, formal, or biblical/literary language, "fowl" can mean any bird whatsoever — sparrows, eagles, pigeons, anything that flies. You may come across phrases like "the fowls of the air" in old texts. This usage is largely archaic (old-fashioned) today. You won't normally hear it in everyday modern speech.

2. The common, everyday meaning — domestic birds raised for food

This is the meaning you'll encounter most often in modern English. Here, "fowl" refers to domesticated (farm-raised) birds that humans keep for their meat, eggs, or feathers. This group includes:

  • Chickens (the most common fowl)
  • Turkeys
  • Ducks
  • Geese
  • Guinea fowl

These are also called poultry, and in fact "fowl" and "poultry" overlap heavily in meaning. If someone says "she kept fowl on her farm," you immediately understand she was raising birds like chickens, ducks, or turkeys.

3. The hunting meaning — wild birds hunted for sport or food

In the context of hunting, "fowl" refers to wild birds that people hunt, such as pheasants, partridges, grouse, and quail. These are sometimes called game birds. A hunter going out to shoot birds might be said to be fowling (the verb form), and the sport is called fowling.
A special culinary meaning: the "boiling fowl"

In cooking, "fowl" has a very specific meaning worth knowing. It often refers to a mature, older bird — typically a hen (female chicken) that has spent its life laying eggs and is then used for cooking once it is no longer productive. This is sometimes called a boiling fowl or stewing fowl.

This older bird is noticeably different from the young chicken you typically see in supermarkets (called a broiler or fryer):

  • A young chicken raised for meat is tender and cooks quickly (roasting, frying).
  • A boiling fowl is tougher, with firmer, more flavourful meat, and needs long, slow cooking (stewing, boiling, slow cookers) to become tender.

When a recipe says "use a boiling fowl," it is specifically asking for this older, harder bird — not a regular young chicken.

This word has a slightly unusual plural. Both forms are correct:

  • Fowl (unchanged) → "He bought three fowl at the market."
  • Fowls (with -s) → "Several fowls escaped from the pen."

Both are standard and acceptable. In practice, the unchanged plural ("three fowl") is slightly more common, especially in formal or older writing.

"Fowl" appears inside several important compound words you will definitely encounter:

  • Waterfowl — birds that live on or near water and swim, such as ducks, geese, and swans. "The lake was full of waterfowl."
  • Wildfowl — wild birds in general, especially those that are hunted. "Wildfowl shooting is popular in the countryside."
  • Guinea fowl — a specific type of domesticated bird, spotted and round, originally from Africa. Often shortened to just "guinea fowl."
  • Peafowl — the group name for peacocks (male) and peahens (female) together.

These two words sound completely identical when spoken aloud, but they are entirely different words with entirely different meanings. This is one of the most common spelling errors in English.

  • Fowl (the bird) → "A chicken is a fowl."
  • Foul (adjective/noun/verb — meaning unpleasant, smelly, or a rule-breaking act in sports) → "That smell is foul." / "The referee called a foul."

A simple way to remember: fowl has a "w" in it, just like the word "wing" — and birds have wings.
Example sentences to see the word in action

• "The farmer woke up early to feed his fowl." (his chickens and ducks)
  • "Chicken is by far the most widely consumed fowl in the world."
  • "The recipe works better with a boiling fowl than a young roasting chicken."
  • "A flock of waterfowl landed on the river at dusk."
  • "In ancient times, the word 'fowl' referred to any bird of the air."
  • "They spent the weekend fowling in the marshes." (hunting wild birds)

ContextWhat "fowl" means

In short: a fowl is a bird, and specifically:

  • In everyday use → a domestic farm bird raised for food (chicken, duck, turkey, etc.)
  • In cooking → often an older, tougher hen meant for slow cooking
  • In hunting → a wild bird hunted for sport or food
  • In old or literary language → any bird at all
  • In compound words → part of "waterfowl," "wildfowl," "peafowl," "guinea fowl"
